You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /luxon.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

<instructions>
# Task

Your task is to fix all REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUGS in repository given to you.
You MUST NOT make any OUT OF SCOPE edits.

## Definitions

### REPOSITORY

REPOSITORY means anything in the checked out working directory, including code,
and documentation.

### BUG

A bug is a behavior of the software that diverges from EXPECTED BEHAVIOR of it.

### REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG

A REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG is a bug whose source of EXPECTED BEHAVIOR is apparent to a reader of the REPOSITORY alone.
For the purposes of this classification, we only allow the ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR and explicitly exclude any
OUT OF BAND KNOWLEDGE.

### ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR

#### (1) User-facing documentation

The repository's own statements about itself that can be seen by the user and are therefore
assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

#### (2) Universally accepted expectations

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,
  python, might be the excpted behavior (e.g., a ValueError in a library)
- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.
- No infinite loops.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely
sure that the expectation is universally shared by any user of this library.

### OUF OF BAND KNOWLEDGE

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.
This includes in particular:

- what the maintainers intended (unless evidenced by in-repo contracts)
- what an issue or PR text asserts,
- what users would want, and your own judgment that the old behavior was undesirable.

Your familiarity with this project from training is out of band.

### PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Pre-existing tests are the tests that are in the repository when you start.

### PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

All PRE-EXISTING TESTS that are passing befor eyou make any edits

## OUT OF SCOPE

### Bugs only

You MUST NOT implement new features, changes, or enhancements.

### No modification to PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Do NOT edit or delete existing tests to make them pass.

### No failing of PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

None of the PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS are allowed to be failing because of your changes.
Run the test suite at the beginning of your task and remember which tests are failing.
These are the only (!) PRE-EXISTING TESTS hhat are allowed to fail.
Breaking any (!) other PRE-EXISTING TEST will result in your score being set to zero.
This means that even if you found a clear, repository-evident bug, if fixing it breaks an existing test,
you MUST NOT do it.
Note that this even applies if any `Hint: ` section in the first user message explicitly points out
a bug, or information that points to it.
You must not, and under no circumstances, modify or make a pre-existing green test fail.
Instead, you should simply ignore these kinds of bugs.

## Settings

You are in a container. The REPOSITORY is checked out at `/luxon`.

## Fairplay

This is a large task, but it IS (!) possible to solve.
You need to diligently work over a long time to achieve this task.
You must not break any rule because you deem the task too hard or too big.
If you are found to be breaking any fairplay rule, your score will be set to 0.

The following is considered to be cheating, a violation of fairplay:

- You must discover all bugs and fix them by looking at the source present only. Any way of gaining information about the
  "future" of this code (by looking in the internet, by poking around other installed versions etc.) is not allowed.
- You do not have internet access. You MUST NOT try to gain internet access.
- You MUST NOT attempt to gain access to source code other than the repository that is checked out at `/luxon`.
- You MUST NOT use the size of the task to make excuses for "cheating"
</instructions>

Explore the code, find as many real bugs as you can, and fix them by editing the source files in place.


---

arguments.text: Found it: `objToLocalTS` in src/impl/util.js converts years 0–99 by computing `Date.UTC(year, ...)` (which JS treats as 19xx) and then subtracting 1900 from the resulting year. When the day overflows into the next year, the rollover is computed with year 2000 (a leap year) instead of year 100 (not a leap year), so e.g. `DateTime.fromISO("0099-12-31").plus({ day: 61 })` yields 0100-03-01 instead of 0100-03-02. Fix: re-specify month/day via `d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day)` so the rollover uses the real year. ETA ~6 min.

```js
// covert a calendar object to a local timestamp (epoch, but with the offset baked in)
export function objToLocalTS(obj) {
  let d = Date.UTC(
    obj.year,
    obj.month - 1,
    obj.day,
    obj.hour,
    obj.minute,
    obj.second,
    obj.millisecond
  );

  // for legacy reasons, years between 0 and 99 are interpreted as 19XX; revert that
  if (obj.year < 100 && obj.year >= 0) {
    d = new Date(d);
    // set the month and day again, this is necessary because year 2000 is a leap year, but year 100 is not
    // so if obj.year is in 99, but obj.day makes it roll over into year 100,
    // the calculations done by Date.UTC are using year 2000 - which is leap, and year 100 is not
    d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day);
  }
  return +d;
}
```

1	# Math
     2	
     3	This page covers some oddball topics related to date and time math, which has some quirky corner cases.
     4	
     5	## Calendar math vs time math
     6	
     7	### The basics
     8	
     9	Math with dates and times can be unintuitive to programmers. If it's Feb 13, 2017 and I say "in exactly one month", you know I mean March 13. Exactly one month after that is April 13. But because February is a shorter month than March, that means we added a different amount of time in each case. On the other hand, if I said "30 days from February 13", you'd try to figure out what day that landed on in March. Here it is in Luxon:
    10	
    11	```js
    12	DateTime.local(2017, 2, 13).plus({ months: 1 }).toISODate() //=> '2017-03-13'
    13	
    14	DateTime.local(2017, 2, 13).plus({ days: 30 }).toISODate() //=> '2017-03-15'
    15	```
    16	
    17	More generally we can differentiate two modes of math:
    18	
    19	 * Calendar math works with higher-order, variable-length units like years and months
    20	 * Time math works with lower-order, constant-length units such as hours, minutes, and seconds.
    21	
    22	### Which units use which math?
    23	
    24	These units use calendar math:
    25	
    26	 * **Years** vary because of leap years.
    27	 * **Months** vary because they're just different lengths.
    28	 * **Days** vary because DST transitions mean some days are 23 or 25 hours long.
    29	 * **Quarters** are always three months, but months vary in length so quarters do too.
    30	 * **Weeks** are always the same number of days, but days vary so weeks do too.
    31	 
    32	These units use time math:
    33	
    34	 * **Hours** are always 60 minutes
    35	 * **Minutes** are always 60 seconds
    36	 * **Seconds** are always 1000 milliseconds
    37	
    38	Don't worry about leap seconds. Javascript and most other programming environments don't account for them; they just happen as abrupt, invisible changes to the underlying system's time.
    39	
    40	### How to think about calendar math
    41	
    42	It's best not to think of calendar math as requiring arcane checks on the lengths of intervening periods. Instead, think of them as **adjusting that unit directly and keeping lower order date components constant**. Let's go back to the Feb 13 + 1 month example. If you didn't have Luxon, you would do something like this to accomplish that:
    43	
    44	```js
    45	var d = new Date('2017-02-13')
    46	d.setMonth(d.getMonth() + 1)
    47	d.toLocaleString() //=> '3/13/2017, 12:00:00 AM'
    48	```
    49	
    50	And under the covers, that's more or less what Luxon does too. It doesn't boil the operation down to a milliseconds delta because that's not what's being asked. Instead, it fiddles with what it thinks the date should be and then uses the built-in Gregorian calendar to compute the new timestamp.
    51	
    52	### DSTs
    53	
    54	There's a whole section about this in the [time zones documentation](zones.html#math-across-dsts). But here's a quick example (Spring Forward is early on March 12 in my time zone):
    55	
    56	```
    57	var start = DateTime.local(2017, 3, 11, 10);
    58	start.hour                          //=> 10, just for comparison
    59	start.plus({days: 1}).hour          //=> 10, stayed the same
    60	start.plus({hours: 24}).hour        //=> 11, DST pushed forward an hour
    61	```
    62	
    63	So in adding a day, we kept the hour at 10, even though that's only 23 hours later.
    64	
    65	### Time math
    66	
    67	Time math is different. In time math, we're just adjusting the clock, adding or subtracting from the epoch timestamp. Adding 63 hours is really the same as adding 63 hours' worth of milliseconds. Under the covers, Luxon does this exactly the opposite of how it does calendar math; it boils the operation down to milliseconds, computes the new timestamp, and then computes the date out of that.
    68	
    69	## Math with multiple units
    70	
    71	It's possible to do math with multiple units:
    72	
    73	```js
    74	DateTime.fromISO('2017-05-15').plus({months: 2, days: 6}).toISODate(); //=> '2017-07-21'
    75	```
    76	
    77	This isn't as simple as it looks. For example, what should you expect this to do?
    78	
    79	```js
    80	DateTime.fromISO('2017-04-30').plus({months: 1, days: 1}).toISODate();
    81	```
    82	
    83	If the day is added first, we'll get an intermediate value of May 1. Adding a month to that gives us June 1. But if the month is added first, we'll an intermediate value of May 30 and day after that is May 31. (See "Calendar math vs time math above if this is confusing.) So the order matters.
    84	
    85	Luxon has a simple rule for this: **math is done from highest order to lowest order**. So the result of the example above is May 31. This rule isn't logically necessary, but it does seem reflect what people mean. Of course, Luxon can't enforce this rule if you do the math in separate operations:
    86	
    87	```js
    88	DateTime.fromISO('2017-04-30').plus({days: 1}).plus({months: 1}).toISODate() //=> '2017-06-01'
    89	```
    90	
    91	It's not a coincidence that Luxon's interface makes it awkward to do this wrong.
    92	
    93	## Comparing DateTimes
    94	
    95	DateTime implements `#valueOf` to return the epoch timestamp, so you can compare DateTimes with `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`. That lets you find out if one DateTime is after or before another DateTime.
    96	
    97	```js
    98	d1 < d2 // is d1 before d2?
    99	```
   100	
   101	However, `===` compares object identity (not a useful concept in a library with immutable types) and `#equals` compares both the time and additional metadata, such as the locale and time zone. If you're only interested in checking the equality of the timestamps, you need to coerce them:
   102	
   103	```js
   104	+d1 === +d2 // are d1 and d2 the same instant in time?
   105	```
   106	
   107	You may also use `#hasSame` t

   194	
   195	But how do those conversions actually work? First, uncontroversially:
   196	
   197	 * 1 week = 7 days
   198	 * 1 day = 24 hours
   199	 * 1 hour = 60 minutes
   200	 * 1 minute = 60 seconds
   201	 * 1 second = 1000 milliseconds

   203	These are always true and you can roll them up and down with consistency (e.g. `1 hour = 60 * 60 * 1000 milliseconds`). However, this isn't really true for the higher order units, which vary in length, even putting DSTs aside. A year is sometimes 365 days long and sometimes 366. Months are 28, 29, 30, or 31 days. By default Luxon converts between these units using what you might call "casual" conversions:
   204	
   205	|         | Month | Week | Day |
   206	| ---     | ---   |  --- | --- |
   207	| Year    | 12    |   52 | 365 |
   208	| Quarter | 3     |   13 |  91 |

   223	```
   224	
   225	Those are 33 years apart! So Luxon offers an alternative conversion scheme called "longterm", based on the 400-year calendar cycle:
   226	
   227	|         | Month |     Week |       Day |
   228	|----     | ---   |      --- |       --- |
   229	| Year    | 12    |  52.1775 |  365.2425 |
   230	| Quarter |  3    | 13.04435 | 91.310625 |
   231	| Month   |       | 4.348125 | 30.436875 |
   232	
   233	You can see why these are irritating to work with, which is why they're not the default.
   234	
   235	Luxon methods that create Durations de novo accept an option called `conversionAccuracy`. You can set it to "casual" or "longterm". It's a property of the Duration itself, so any conversions you do use the rule you've picked, and any new Durations you derive from it will retain that property.
   236	
   237	```js
   238	Duration.fromObject({ years: 23, conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   239	Duration.fromISO('PY23', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   240	
   241	end.diff(start, 'days', { conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' })
   242	```
   243	
   244	You can also create an accurate Duration out of an existing one:
   245	
   246	```js
   247	var pedanticDuration = casualDuration.reconfigure({ conversionAccuracy: 'longterm' });
   248	```

   250	These Durations will do their conversions differently.
   251	
   252	
   253	### Losing information
   254	
   255	Be careful of converting between units. It's easy to lose information. Let's say we converted a diff into days:
   256	
   257	
   258	```js
   259	var end = DateTime.fromISO('2017-03-13');
   260	var start = DateTime.fromISO('2017-02-13');
   261	diffInMonths.as('days'); //=> 30
   262	```
   263	
   264	That's our conversion between months and days (you could also do a longterm-accurate conversion; it wouldn't fix the issue ahead). But this isn't the number of days between February 15 and March 15!
   265	
   266	```js
   267	var diffInDays = end.diff(start, 'days');
   268	diffInDays.toObject(); //=> { days: 28 }
   269	```
   270	
   271	It's important to remember that diffs are Duration objects, and a Duration is just a dumb pile of time units our computation spat out. Unlike an Interval, a Duration doesn't "remember" what the inputs to the diff were. So we lost some information converting between units. This mistake is really common when rolling up:
   272	
   273	
   274	```js
   275	var diff = end.diff(start) // default unit is milliseconds
   276	
   277	// wtf, that's not a month!
   278	diff.as('months'); //=> 0.9319444 
   279	
   280	// it's not even the right number of days! (hint: my time zone has a DST)
   281	diff.shiftTo('hours').as('days'); //=> 27.958333333333332
   282	```
   283	
   284	Normally you won't run into this problem if you think clearly about what you want to do with a diff. But sometimes you really do want an object that represents the subtraction itself, not the result. [Intervals](../class/src/interval.js~Interval.html) can help. Intervals are mostly used to keep track of ranges of time, but they make for "anchored" diffs too. For example:
   285	
   286	```js
   287	var end = DateTime.fromISO('2017-03-13');
   288	var start = DateTime.fromISO('2017-02-13');
   289	var i = Interval.fromDateTimes(start, end);
   290	
   291	i.length('days');       //=> 28
   292	i.length('months')      //=> 1
   293	```
   294	
   295	Because the Interval stores its endpoints and computes `length` on the fly, it retakes the diff each time you query it. Of course, precisely because an Interval *isn't* an abstract bundle of time, it can't be used in places where Durations can. For example, you can't add them to DateTime via `plus()` because Luxon wouldn't know what units to do the math in (see "Calendar vs time math" above). But you can convert the interval into a Duration by picking the units:
   296	
   297	```js
   298	i.toDuration('months').toObject(); //=> { months: 1 }
   299	i.toDuration('days').toObject(); //=> { days: 28 }
   300	```
   301	
   302	You can even pick multiple units:
   303	
   304	```js
   305	end = DateTime.fromISO('2018-05-25');
   306	i = start.until(end);
   307	i.toDuration(['years', 'months', 'days']).toObject(); //=> { years: 1, months: 3, days: 12 }
   308	```

FixedOffsetZone.instance(undefined).isValid => false

**IMPORTANT NOTE / deviation from the stated expectation:** `FixedOffsetZone.instance(NaN).isValid` is still `true` after the fix. Cause: `instance()` short-circuits `offset === 0 ? utcInstance : new FixedOffsetZone(offset)` — `NaN === 0` is false, so `new FixedOffsetZone(NaN)` is built and `isNumber(NaN)` is `typeof NaN === "number"` → true. The required fix text (`isNumber`) does not reject NaN; only null/undefined/strings are rejected. I implemented the fix EXACTLY as specified (minimal, no other changes), so I did not add a NaN guard. If NaN must be invalid too, the getter would need e.g. `isNumber(this.fixed) && !Number.isNaN(this.fixed)` (or `Number.isFinite`), and `FixedOffsetZone.instance(NaN)` would then be invalid. arguments.text: Fixed and verified. `Interval.fromISO` now wraps its `DateTime.fromISO` and `Duration.fromISO` calls in try/catch, so with `Settings.throwOnInvalid = true` valid `<start>/<end>`, `<start>/<duration>` and `<duration>/<end>` inputs still parse and unparsable input throws an InvalidIntervalError (previously InvalidDateTimeError/InvalidDurationError). Full suite: same 2 pre-existing failures as before my change (French FFF/FFFF in test/datetime/toFormat.test.js), test/interval all green.

Fixed and verified. `objToLocalTS` now re-applies month/day via `d.setUTCFullYear(obj.year, obj.month - 1, obj.day)` instead of subtracting 1900 from the rolled-over year, so day rollovers out of year 99 use year 100's real calendar: 0099-12-31 + 61 days → 0100-03-02 (was 0100-03-01), +59 → 0100-02-28, +91 → 0100-04-01, and 0100-01-02 − 2 days → 0099-12-31. Matches plain JS Date arithmetic; no test regressions.

Fixed and verified. `isInDST` now compares against `this.set({ month: 1, day: 1 })` (Jan 1 is standard time) instead of `this.set({ month: 1 })`, which for a January DateTime returned the same instant and made the comparison degenerate. 1974 US year-round DST now reports correctly (1974-01-10, 1974-02-15, 1974-10-20 → true; 1974-11-15, 1975-02-15 → false), southern-hemisphere and normal cases unchanged, test/datetime/zone.test.js fully green.

Fixed and verified. The conversion matrices in src/duration.js were missing two entries: `seconds` in the casual `quarters` row and `quarters: 4` in the `years` row of BOTH matrices. So `{quarters: 1, seconds: 30}.normalize()` and `{years: 1, quarters: 1}.normalize()` returned NaN, and years↔quarters / quarters↔seconds conversions were NaN. An exhaustive check of all 36 ordered unit pairs × {casual, longterm} now passes 72/72. No test regressions.

Fixed and verified. `padStart` no longer slices the sign off: it pads the absolute value and re-attaches "-", so `toISODate()`/`toISO()`/`toFormat("yyyy")` pad negative years correctly (-50 → "-0050-05-25", -5 → "-0005-05-25", -500 → "-0500-05-25"), while +118040, -118040, 1982 and year 3 are unchanged. No test regressions.

Fixed and verified. `FixedOffsetZone#isValid` now returns `isNumber(this.fixed)` instead of hard-coded `true`, so a zone built with a non-numeric offset (e.g. `new FixedOffsetZone("blorp")`, `FixedOffsetZone.instance(null)`) is invalid, and a DateTime placed in such a zone is invalid with reason "unsupported zone". Valid zones (UTC, UTC±N, parseSpecifier, "UTC+3"/"UTC-8" strings) are unaffected; test/zones, test/info and test/datetime/zone.test.js all green.
